text: Here’s something strange about AI. Train the exact same model twice, and you can get very different results. Let me show you why.
This is a neural network. A tiny one. Each line is a weight: a number the network adjusts as it learns.
This grey part stands in for a pretrained model, like BERT, which read billions of words of English before anyone gave it a specific job. That’s called pretraining.

Then we fine-tune it on a small, specific job, called a downstream task. Say, deciding whether two sentences mean the same thing. It gets a few practice examples, and a test at the end. That’s the setting of this paper.
For the new job, we attach a new output layer. Its weights start out random. Blue is positive, red is negative. That’s the first roll of the dice.
Now the practice examples. Sixty-four of them, fed in four at a time. Before training, their order is shuffled at random. That’s the second roll of the dice.
Both rolls are controlled by one number: the random seed. Change the seed, and both rolls come out differently.

So let’s train with seed one. The model goes through the examples six times, in a new shuffled order each time, and every weight gets nudged, the pretrained ones too. Then we test it on 400 examples it has never seen.
It gets 78% accuracy: 311 of the 400 test examples right. That orange dot is our result.
Now here’s the experiment. Same network. Same examples. Same settings. We only change the seed.
Let’s run a hundred of them.
Each dot is one complete training run. Most land in the middle, but some seeds are far luckier than others.
The worst run got 60.8%. The best got 82.5%. That’s a 21.7-point gap, and the only thing we changed was the seed.
And this isn’t just a toy. In 2020, researchers fine-tuned BERT 2,100 times across four tasks, and found the same thing. On the small datasets, some runs even failed completely.
So which roll of the dice is doing this? The starting weights, or the order of the examples? The paper gave each roll its own seed, so it could change one at a time. Let’s do the same.
First, we keep the starting weights the same every run, and only shuffle the order.
Just by reordering the same 64 examples, the accuracy moves 11.2 points.
Now the opposite. Keep the order the same, and only reroll the starting weights.
19.0 points. So both of them matter.
The paper found the same thing: on average, the two matter about equally. And some starting weights did well on all four tasks they tried.
Now, here’s why this is a problem. When a paper reports a result, you don’t see a hundred dots. You see one.
Imagine a lab that tries one seed, and reports whatever it gets.
A second lab tries five seeds, and reports only the best one.
A third lab tries twenty.
Same model, same code, and the reported accuracy went up 6.2 points, just from trying more seeds.
And this actually happened. Here are published scores on a benchmark called MRPC.

After 625 seeds, BERT’s best run on this task scored above the published results of XLNet, RoBERTa and ALBERT: newer models that had been reported as better. The paper is careful to note that those models never got 625 tries.
So how do you know if a new method is actually better, or just luckier? Let’s compare two: method A and method B.
A reports one try. B reports its best out of twenty. B looks 6.2 points better. Sounds like a breakthrough, right?
But let’s give A twenty tries as well.
They’re identical. A and B were the same method all along. B just had more tries.
So the fix is simple. Report how many seeds you tried, and compare methods using the same number of tries.
And if you can afford many tries, the paper has a cheaper trick: start lots of runs, and stop the unpromising ones early.
Because one score is just one lottery ticket.
